row.title: How They Broke Away to Go to Rootabaga Country
row.author: Carl Sandburg

plot_extraction.response_text: Tired of living where everything always stays the same, Gimme the Ax and his two self-named children, Please Gimme and Ax Me No Questions, sell all their possessions and buy a special train ticket to travel beyond the end of the railroad. Their journey carries them through fantastical lands where trains pass over and under one another, balloon pickers work on stilts, and circus clowns are baked in ovens and brought to life. Eventually, the tracks begin to zigzag, and they arrive in the Rootabaga Country, where pigs wear patterned bibs and the great city is the Village of Liver-and-Onions.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a playful, orally driven fairy-tale style that combines homespun American speech with exuberant nonsense. Its narrator sounds like a practiced storyteller addressing children directly: confident, conversational, and willing to treat impossibilities as ordinary facts. The opening relies on plain, categorical statements—chimneys let smoke out, doors open, windows are open or shut—before gradually carrying that matter-of-fact logic into a surreal world. This contrast between simple explanation and wild invention is central to the story’s comic effect.

The diction mixes everyday rural and mechanical vocabulary with whimsical coinages. Pigs, pastures, pitchforks, ragbags, railroad stations, whistles, bells, and cash belong to a recognizable folk-Americana setting, while phrases such as “blue spanch,” “steam hog,” “balloon pickers,” and “forty ways farther yet” make the world strange. Names such as Gimme the Ax, Please Gimme, and Ax Me No Questions are built from fragments of colloquial speech, giving the characters the quality of figures in a tall tale or nursery rhyme. Concrete details are preferred to abstract description, but those details are freely recombined into fantastic images: balloons grow like crops, clowns are baked in ovens, and pigs wear patterned bibs.

The syntax is mostly simple, additive, and repetitive. Sentences frequently begin with “And,” “Then,” “Sometimes,” or “When,” creating the forward rhythm of spoken narration. Repeated formulas—“the train ran on and on,” “everything is the same as it always was,” and the full description of the “long slick yellow leather slab ticket with a blue spanch across it”—function like refrains. They make the prose easy to remember, give it ceremonial momentum, and allow small variations to become humorous. Parallel structures and incremental lists are common, as in the catalogues of destinations, balloons, ovens, and patterned pigs.

Sound is especially important. Alliteration appears in clusters such as “pigs, pastures, pepper pickers, pitchforks,” while internal rhyme, repeated consonants, and rhythmic triads give many lines the bounce of verse. Onomatopoeic expressions such as “chick-a-chick” and “pfisty-pfoost” imitate the machinery of the train while turning it into a creature with its own comic personality. Questions often come in threes—“Who’s who? How much? And what’s the answer?” or “So far? So early? So soon?”—and counting patterns such as “once, twice, three times” reinforce the folktale cadence.

The imagery is vivid, primary-coloured, and deliberately illogical. Human features are described through landscape and weather: the children have “shadows of valleys by night” in their eyes, sunrise on their foreheads, and hair like dark wild grass. Personification gives the wind fingers and the train a hog-like nose. Similes remain accessible and visual, comparing zigzagging tracks to repeated letters Z or a clown to a large doll. The fantasy therefore feels tactile and visible rather than ethereal.

Dialogue serves less to create psychologically distinct characters than to establish rhythms, rules, and comic explanations. Children ask literal questions, and the father answers with serene absurdity. His explanations do not resolve the world’s strangeness; they extend it according to dream logic. The deadpan delivery is crucial: no character expresses sustained disbelief when trains pass over and under one another or when songs make a man light enough to float. The narration treats each marvel as part of a coherent local custom.

Structurally, the story moves from confinement to journey. It begins in a house defined by sameness, then uses the railroad as an episodic passage through increasingly fantastic countries. Each episode has a compact pattern: arrival, visual spectacle, a child’s question, and the father’s explanatory answer. The repeated motion of the train links these self-contained scenes. The ending shifts into direct second-person instruction, turning the adventure into practical folklore and inviting the reader to repeat it. It also circles back through the story’s recurring objects and phrases rather than providing conventional closure.

The tone is warm, mischievous, and wonder-filled, with an undercurrent of dissatisfaction with fixed routines. Sameness is answered not by argument but by imaginative departure. Yet the story does not reject rules altogether; it replaces ordinary rules with more delightful ones. Its distinctive style arises from that combination of plainspoken certainty, musical repetition, tall-tale exaggeration, childlike linguistic play, and surreal invention presented as common sense.

generation.response_text:
Chimneys are for letting smoke out. Doors are for going in and coming out. Windows are for looking through, except when they are shut, and then they are for keeping the weather on the weather side.

That was the kind of house where Gimme the Ax lived with his two children, Please Gimme and Ax Me No Questions.

Every morning the same smoke climbed out of the chimney. Every noon the same door opened and shut. Every night the same windows looked at the same moon sitting on the same fence post.

The pigs in the pasture grunted the same grunts. The pepper pickers picked the same peppers. The old red rooster stood on one leg, then the other leg, and never thought of standing on a third leg.

So one morning Gimme the Ax said, “Everything is the same as it always was.”

Please Gimme said, “The spoons are in the spoon box.”

Ax Me No Questions said, “The rain barrel has rain in it.”

“And the railroad goes only as far as the railroad goes,” said Gimme the Ax. “I am tired of living where everything is the same as it always was.”

He took a pitchfork and sold it to a man who collected pitchfork shadows. He sold the rain barrel to a woman who needed a round place to keep square rain. He sold the pigs, the pasture, the pepper patch, the spoon box, the chimney smoke, and the squeak out of the front door.

The man who bought the squeak put it in his pocket. Every time he sat down, his pocket opened and said, “Squeee-ick.”

Last of all, Gimme the Ax sold the house to the moon. The moon paid cash because the moon had no pockets for promises.

Then Gimme the Ax and Please Gimme and Ax Me No Questions put their clothes in three ragbags and went to the railroad station.

At the ticket window sat a man with one green eye and one eye the colour of Tuesday afternoon.

“How far do you want to go?” he asked.

“Farther than far,” said Gimme the Ax.

“So far? So early? So soon?” asked the ticket man.

“Farther than the end of the railroad,” said Gimme the Ax.

The ticket man opened a drawer. Inside were red tickets for near places, white tickets for winter places, and small round tickets for people travelling in circles. Under all these he found a long slick yellow leather slab ticket with a blue spanch across it.

“This is the ticket,” he said. “It goes to the end of the railroad, and then forty ways farther yet.”

“How much?” asked Please Gimme.

“Who’s who? How much? And what’s the answer?” said the ticket man. “It costs everything you have left, except your names.”

Gimme the Ax poured their money on the counter. There were seven dollars, nine nickels, eleven pennies, and one button pretending to be a dime.

The ticket man took the money and left the button.

“You may need it,” he said. “Beyond the end of the railroad, buttons are sometimes elected mayor.”

They climbed aboard a train with a steam hog nose on the engine. Its bell went bong-bing, its wheels went chick-a-chick, and its whistle cried, “Pfisty-pfoost! Pfisty-pfoost! Anybody staying home had better stay home!”

And the train ran on and on.

It ran past wheat fields combing their yellow hair. It ran past barns with red shoulders. It ran past a town where all the dogs were named Monday because nobody liked to call them Sunday.

Then the tracks began climbing.

Up in the air ran another railroad. Under that railroad ran another one, and under that one ran two more. Trains crossed over trains and under trains. One train went east while facing west. Another stood still so fast that sparks flew from its wheels.

Please Gimme looked out the window.

“Which train is on top?” she asked.

“The top one when you look from the bottom,” said Gimme the Ax. “But if you stand on top, the bottom one is on top of your looking.”

Ax Me No Questions pointed at a silver engine rolling upside down beneath a bridge.

“Why don’t the people fall out?”

“They paid extra to fall up,” said Gimme the Ax.

The silver engine rang its bell three times—once for over, twice for under, three times for neither—and away it went carrying six barrels of sunrise and a lady with a blue goose in her hat.

And the train ran on and on.

Toward evening they came to a country where balloons grew in fields.

Red balloons hung from low bushes. Blue balloons grew on tall vines. Green balloons slept under broad leaves until the wind tickled them awake. Yellow balloons rose from the earth on stems so thin a grasshopper could tie them in a knot.

Men and women walked between the rows on stilts. They carried long-handled balloon hooks and wore cloud-coloured mittens.

“Balloon pickers,” said Gimme the Ax before anybody asked.

One picker hooked a purple balloon, twisted it once, twice, three times, and dropped it into a wagon. The wagon floated six inches above the road.

“What happens if a balloon gets too ripe?” asked Please Gimme.

“It leaves home,” said Gimme the Ax.

Just then a ripe orange balloon broke from its stem. It sailed over the field with the wind’s fingers pushing its round sides.

A balloon picker took off his hat.

“Good luck!” he shouted. “Write if you land anywhere!”

“Where do they sell the balloons?” asked Ax Me No Questions.

“At the sky market,” said Gimme the Ax. “They sell the small ones to birthdays and the big ones to sunsets.”

The train whistle went pfisty-pfoost, and the balloon pickers waved their long hooks. One hook caught the last car and stretched it as long as a piece of warm taffy. Then it snapped loose, and the car sprang back with every passenger sitting in somebody else’s seat.

And the train ran on and on.

At midnight they reached a town smelling of sawdust, cinnamon, hot iron, and red paint.

There stood seven ovens in a row. They were tall ovens with brass doors and thermometers shaped like smiling mouths. Men in white aprons rolled wheelbarrows back and forth. In the wheelbarrows lay flour, buttons, striped socks, red rubber noses, and jars of canned laughter.

“What do they bake here?” asked Please Gimme.

“Circus clowns,” said Gimme the Ax.

A baker poured flour into a wooden bowl. He added two striped socks, a fistful of freckles, three spoons of canned laughter, and one red rubber nose. Then he stirred it all with a broomstick.

“Too serious,” said another baker.

So they added six tickles and a feather.

They rolled the dough into a shape like a large doll, buttoned a purple coat around it, and slid it into the third oven.

“How long does a clown bake?” asked Ax Me No Questions.

“Until the shoes turn up at the toes,” said Gimme the Ax.

The oven clock struck once, twice, three times, and the brass door flew open. Out stepped a hot new clown with sunrise on his forehead, a whistle in his ear, and green squares painted on his knees.

He bowed to the bakers. He bowed to the train. Then he tripped over nothing and fell upward into a barrel.

The bakers clapped.

“A good batch,” they said.

Next came a little clown baked too light. He floated above the ground like thistle fuzz.

“Sing him heavy,” called the head baker.

So the bakers sang:

“Boots full of buckles,  
Pockets full of stones,  
Soup in the elbows,  
Gravy in the bones.”

The clown drifted down and landed softly on his enormous shoes.

“Why did the song make him heavy?” asked Please Gimme.

“Because the tune was carrying too much gravy,” said Gimme the Ax.

They left the bakers loading twelve fresh clowns into a circus wagon. Each clown had a paper label tied to one ear: HANDLE WITH LAUGHTER.

And the train ran on and on.

In the morning there were no telegraph poles. At noon there were no fences. By afternoon the track itself looked undecided.

First it went straight.

Then it bent left.

Then it bent right.

Then it made a sharp Z, a sleepy Z, and a crooked Z with one corner missing.

The engine shook its steam hog nose. Chick-a-chick went the wheels. Pfisty-pfoost went the whistle. The track zigged and zagged, and the train zagged when it should have zigged and zigged when there was no zig to zag.

“Are we lost?” asked Ax Me No Questions.

“A straight track can be lost,” said Gimme the Ax. “A zigzag track always knows two ways home.”

The track made seven more Z’s. It wrote Z Z Z across a brown prairie, climbed a blue hill, ducked under a river, and came up dripping fish scales.

Then they saw pigs.

There were little pigs and big pigs, pink pigs and black pigs, pigs with curly tails and pigs whose tails had forgotten to curl. Every pig wore a bib.

One wore a red bib with yellow stars. One wore a blue bib with silver spoons. One wore a checkerboard bib, and another wore a bib printed all over with tiny green locomotives.

A tall pig in a striped bib stood beside the track ringing a handbell.

“Why do the pigs wear bibs?” asked Please Gimme.

“This is the Rootabaga Country,” said Gimme the Ax. “Here the mud is clean, but breakfast is careless.”

The tall pig rang his bell again.

“Tickets, names, buttons, and reasons for arriving!” he called.

Gimme the Ax showed him the long slick yellow leather slab ticket with a blue spanch across it.

The pig looked at the ticket from the front. He looked at it from the back. He smelled the blue spanch.

“Beyond-the-end passengers,” he said. “You have come forty ways farther yet.”

Gimme the Ax gave him the button the ticket man had returned.

“Is this the mayor?” asked the pig.

“Not yet,” said Gimme the Ax.

“Then it has time,” said the pig, putting the button carefully into his bib pocket.

The train went past pastures where pitchforks grew with their handles down. It went past ragbags hanging from trees and kicking their empty legs in the wind. It went past steam hogs sleeping in puddles, each one snoring a small white cloud.

At last they saw the great city.

It was called the Village of Liver-and-Onions.

Its streets were purple boards laid end to end. Its houses had green chimneys for letting green smoke out. Its doors opened sideways on Tuesdays and upside down on all other days. Its windows were open or shut, except the polite windows, which winked.

Bells rang from the towers: bong-bing, bing-bong, bingle-bangle-bong.

The people came running to meet the train. There were balloon menders, clown coolers, zigzag measurers, pig-bib buttoners, and three old women who carried tomorrow in covered baskets.

“Is everything always the same here?” asked Please Gimme.

“No,” said a balloon mender. “Sometimes everything is different.”

“And sometimes,” said a clown cooler, “different is the same thing wearing another hat.”

Gimme the Ax looked at his children. In their eyes were shadows of valleys by night. On their foreheads lay the first stripe of sunrise. Their hair blew like dark wild grass where no fence had ever learned to stand.

“This will do,” he said.

So if you are tired of the same chimney smoke, the same spoon box, the same rooster changing from one leg to the other, sell what can be sold and fold what can be folded.

Go to the railroad station.

Ask for the long slick yellow leather slab ticket with a blue spanch across it.

Ride past the trains over trains and under trains. Wave to the balloon pickers. Smell the ovens where the clowns are baked. Wait for the track to zig once, zag twice, and Z three times.

And when a pig in a patterned bib asks your name, tell it plainly.

Keep one button in your pocket.

You may need it for a mayor.

free_generation.response_text:
# The Museum of Lost Hours

At the end of Bellweather Street, where the paving stones sloped toward the river and the fog gathered even on clear mornings, there stood a narrow building with a blue door.

Above the door hung a tarnished brass sign:

**THE MUSEUM OF LOST HOURS**  
**Open from Dawn until Remembered**

Most people passed without noticing it. Some saw the door but mistook the building for a clockmaker’s shop. Others read the sign and laughed, assuming it was a joke left over from some forgotten festival.

Mara Vale had walked past it twice a day for eleven years.

She noticed it only on the morning she was late for her father’s funeral.

The delay was not her fault. A delivery cart had overturned on St. Anne’s Bridge, scattering oranges across the road. Buses stopped, horns complained, and pedestrians darted between rolling fruit. By the time Mara reached the station, the train had already gone.

The next one would leave in an hour.

An hour.

She stood beneath the station clock, staring at the black hands. If she waited, she would arrive after the service. She imagined the chapel emptying, umbrellas blooming in the rain, condolences offered to cousins she barely knew. She imagined her father’s coffin lowered while she sat behind a fogged train window.

He had waited for her often enough.

At school gates. Outside cinemas. Beside hospital beds. Once, for nearly six hours, at an airport after her flight was canceled and her telephone died. He had always been there, holding his old gray coat closed with one hand, saying, “No trouble, Magpie. I’ve got time.”

Mara had not seen him in eight months.

Their last conversation had ended with her hanging up.

She left the station and began to walk, though she did not know where she was going. Her shoes struck the wet stones too hard. She passed the bakery, the boarded theater, the alley where someone had painted silver wings on a brick wall.

Then she saw the blue door.

It was the color of evening just before the stars appeared.

The brass sign trembled in the wind.

Mara stopped.

From inside came the soft, irregular ticking of many clocks.

She tried the handle.

The door opened.

A brass bell gave a single note above her head. The sound did not fade so much as drift away, deeper into the building.

Inside, the museum was larger than it could possibly have been. A hall stretched beyond sight, lined with cabinets, shelves, drawers, and glass cases. Clocks covered the walls: grandfather clocks, carriage clocks, kitchen clocks, watches no bigger than coins. None showed the same time.

The air smelled of dust, rain, and extinguished candles.

Behind a desk sat an old woman in a green velvet jacket. Her white hair was braided down her back, and a jeweler’s lens rested over one eye. She was using silver tweezers to place something bright into a paper envelope.

“Good morning,” she said. “Or good evening. We get both in here.”

“I’m sorry,” Mara said. “I thought this was a clock shop.”

“People often do.”

The woman sealed the envelope and wrote on it in blue ink.

**Seven minutes spent watching snow fall upward. Oslo, 1983.**

Mara read the label twice.

“What is this place?”

The old woman removed the lens from her eye. Her eyes were very dark and unexpectedly kind.

“It is what the sign says.”

“That doesn’t mean anything.”

“Most true things don’t, at first.”

Mara almost turned around. She had no patience for riddles, not today. Then the station clock returned to her mind, its hands moving with perfect indifference.

“My train left without me,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I’m going to miss my father’s funeral.”

“Yes.”

The woman folded her hands.

Mara felt anger rise, sudden and sharp. “Is that all you can say?”

“No. I can also say you have forty-seven minutes before the next train, which will reach Foxmere at twelve sixteen, provided the signal near Hallow Junction behaves itself. The service begins at eleven thirty. You will miss the hymns, the eulogy, and most of the rain.”

Mara stared at her.

“How do you know that?”

“This is a museum of time. Train schedules are hardly our greatest mystery.”

“Then give me an hour.”

The clocks seemed to hesitate.

The old woman’s expression did not change. “I beg your pardon?”

“Give me an hour. If you really have lost time stored here, let me have some.”

“Lost hours cannot simply be handed across a desk like umbrellas.”

“Why not?”

“Because they belong to someone.”

“I’ll buy one.”

“They are not for sale.”

“I’ll return it.”

“No one returns an hour.”

Mara leaned toward the desk. “Please.”

The word came out smaller than she intended.

The old woman studied her face.

“What is your name?”

“Mara Vale.”

“And what would you do with the hour, Mara Vale?”

“Catch the train.”

“That takes five minutes, if we choose the right hour. What would you do with the rest?”

Mara opened her mouth.

She imagined entering the chapel before the coffin arrived. She imagined relatives turning toward her. She would sit in the front pew and bow her head at the proper moments. She would hear a polished version of her father’s life spoken by a priest who had met him three times.

“I don’t know,” she admitted.

The old woman nodded, as if this answer mattered.

“My name is Orra,” she said. “I am the curator. Come with me.”

She rose and opened a gate beside the desk.

Mara glanced back at the blue door.

“Does time pass outside while I’m in here?”

“Not in the usual way.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It is the only one we have.”

Orra led her through the hall.

The first gallery held thousands of small glass bottles. Light shimmered inside them in different colors: pale gold, winter blue, the red of sunset through closed eyelids.

“Minutes,” Orra explained. “Most lost time comes in small quantities.”

“Lost how?”

Orra pointed to a bottle labeled **Four minutes waiting for water to boil.**

“Impatience,” she said. Then to another: **Eleven minutes hiding from a summer storm beneath a pear tree.** “Forgetfulness.”

They passed shelves of boxes and drawers.

**Half an hour spent searching for spectacles already being worn.**

**Twenty-three minutes between waking from a nightmare and feeling safe again.**

**One hour beside a telephone that never rang.**

Mara slowed at that one. The hour was kept in a dark wooden box with a latch shaped like a hand.

“Who did it belong to?”

“We do not display names unless they are given willingly.”

“Can the owner come back for it?”

“Sometimes.”

“And then?”

“We let them visit.”

“Visit?”

“Recovered time cannot be changed. It can only be entered.”

Mara looked down the endless gallery. “You mean people can relive it?”

“Not relive. Witness.”

“That sounds worse.”

“Often it is.”

They turned into a room filled with doors.

Some were tall and elegant, others plain. One was painted yellow and covered in a child’s drawings. Another was burned around the edges. Behind every door came a faint sound: laughter, rain, footsteps, breathing.

Orra stopped before a red door with a brass number seven.

“This hour was lost by a violinist named Emil Sar.”

“How?”

“He spent it sitting beside his sleeping mother. He remembered the important parts—her illness, the hospital, her final words—but forgot this hour entirely. Grief can swallow time whole.”

“Why are you showing me?”

“Because you asked for an hour.”

Orra opened the door.

On the other side was a small hospital room lit by dawn. A young man sat beside a narrow bed, holding a violin case between his knees. His mother slept beneath a white blanket. A vase of daffodils stood on the windowsill.

Mara remained at the threshold.

“Can they see us?”

“No.”

The young man opened his violin case. He tightened the bow, then began to play so quietly the music seemed woven from breath.

His mother did not wake.

Nothing else happened.

Mara watched for what felt like ten minutes. Perhaps it was longer. The music was hesitant at first, then warm and sure. The mother’s hand rested palm-up on the blanket. Near the end of the piece, the young man set down the violin and placed his hand over hers.

The room brightened with morning.

Then it was empty.

Mara found herself back in the gallery. Orra closed the red door.

“That hour is intact,” the curator said. “It can be witnessed because nothing was taken from it. If you use it to alter your own day, it will cease to belong to Emil. His lost hour will become yours.”

“He forgot it anyway.”

“Do forgotten things stop belonging to us?”

Mara thought of her father’s house, which would now be filled with objects waiting to be sorted. His chipped blue cup. His gardening boots. The narrow bed where he had slept. Things he no longer needed, yet which no one else could claim without changing them.

“I only need enough time to reach the train,” she said.

“Five minutes stolen may weigh more than an hour freely given.”

“Then show me one that was freely given.”

Orra’s eyebrows lifted.

“Everything here was lost,” she said. “Nothing was donated.”

They continued through the museum.

They passed the Hall of Sleepless Nights, where hours floated near the ceiling like dim moons. They crossed the Corridor of Postponed Apologies. It was so long Mara could not see the end.

At an iron staircase, Orra began to climb.

“Where are we going?”

“To your collection.”

Mara stopped with one foot on the first step. “My what?”

“Everyone has one.”

“I’ve never been here.”

“That is not required.”

The staircase wound upward through shadows. At the top was an attic crowded with filing cabinets. Rain tapped against the roof, though the sky visible through the round window was clear.

Orra walked between rows until she found a gray cabinet marked V.

She opened a drawer.

Inside were dozens of envelopes, bottles, tins, and boxes. Each bore Mara’s name.

Orra handed her a small envelope.

**Three minutes listening to your father knock, 14 November, fifteen years ago.**

Mara’s fingers tightened.

She remembered that night. She had been seventeen and furious because her father had forbidden her from going to a party. She had locked her bedroom door. He came up later and knocked, asking if she wanted tea.

She had stayed silent until he went away.

“I didn’t lose this,” she said. “I remember it.”

“You remember the fact. The minutes themselves are here.”

Orra handed her another.

**Two hours driving north in silence, after your mother left.**

Another:

**Nine minutes while your father tried to explain why he sold his piano.**

Another:

**Thirty-one seconds before ending the final telephone call.**

Mara dropped it.

The tiny glass vial struck the floor but did not break. Inside it, a thread of white light twisted like smoke.

“I want to leave.”

“The door is downstairs.”

Mara turned toward the staircase, but Orra did not move.

“What happened during the call?” the curator asked.

“You know, apparently.”

“I know only what was lost.”

Mara stared at the vial on the floor.

Her father had telephoned on a Tuesday evening. She had been at work, preparing a presentation for an important client. He said he had been feeling tired. He said the doctor wanted more tests.

Mara told him she was busy.

He made a joke about getting old. She told him not everything was a joke.

Then he asked whether she would come home that weekend.

She said, “You always do this.”

“Do what, Magpie?”

“Make me feel guilty for having a life.”

There had been a pause. Thirty-one seconds, perhaps. She remembered watching the cursor blink on her computer screen.

Then her father said, “That’s not what I want.”

“I have to go.”

“All right.”

She ended the call.

He never called again.

A neighbor found him two weeks later after seeing newspapers piled outside his door. The doctor said his heart had failed quickly. Mara told herself there would have been no warning. She told herself he should have called again. She told herself many things because the truth was only one thing, and she could not bear to look directly at it.

“Can I enter that time?” she asked.

Orra picked up the vial.

“You may witness it.”

“Can I change it?”

“No.”

“Then what’s the point?”

“The point is not always change.”

Orra pressed the vial between her palms.

The attic disappeared.

Mara stood in her office. Her former self sat at a desk, telephone against her ear. Beyond the windows, the city burned with evening light.

“You always do this,” the younger Mara said.

Her voice was colder than Mara remembered.

The conversation unfolded exactly as she knew it would. Then came the silence.

Thirty-one seconds.

But it was not empty.

Through the telephone, faint and far away, Mara heard her father breathing. She heard the creak of his kitchen chair. A clock ticked in the background. Once he tried to speak, but stopped.

The younger Mara rolled her eyes and looked at an email.

Far away, her father whispered, “I’m frightened.”

So softly that the telephone did not carry it.

Mara stepped forward.

“Dad?”

Neither of them heard her.

Her father drew a slow breath. When he spoke again, his voice was lighter.

“That’s not what I want.”

“I have to go,” said her younger self.

“All right.”

The call ended.

The office vanished.

Mara stood in the attic with both hands over her mouth.

“I didn’t know,” she said.

“No,” Orra replied.

“He didn’t tell me.”

“No.”

“Why didn’t he tell me?”

“Perhaps he wanted to spare you. Perhaps he was ashamed. Perhaps courage failed him. Love and fear make poor translators.”

Mara began to cry.

She cried angrily at first, wiping each tear away as if it had offended her. Then her knees gave way, and she sat on the attic floor among the cabinets of lost time.

Orra waited.

“I could have gone home,” Mara said. “I had eight months.”

“Yes.”

“I thought there would be another call.”

“Yes.”

“I thought there was time.”

Orra sat beside her. “Everyone does.”

For a while, only the rain spoke.

At last Mara looked toward the drawer bearing her name.

“How much have I lost?”

“More than some. Less than others.”

“Can I see one more?”

Orra considered this, then reached deep into the drawer and removed a round tin. Its label was faded.

**Forty-seven minutes in a railway café, age six.**

Mara shook her head. “I don’t remember that.”

“Precisely.”

Orra opened the tin.

The attic filled with sunlight.

Mara was six years old again, sitting at a café table in a station she did not recognize. Her legs swung above the floor. A paper crown rested crookedly on her head.

Across from her sat her father, young and dark-haired.

Two trains had been canceled because of snow. Around them, stranded passengers complained at the ticket counter. Her father had bought one cup of tea for himself and a currant bun for Mara. He was turning the delay into a game.

“Where do you think they’re going?” he asked, pointing to an elderly couple.

“To the moon,” little Mara said.

“With those suitcases?”

“They need moon clothes.”

“Of course. Silly me.”

He pointed to a woman in a fur hat.

“Secret queen,” Mara declared.

A tired soldier became a dragon hunter. A ticket inspector became a spy. The café windows fogged, and snow erased the tracks outside.

Mara watched her father tear a paper napkin into the shape of a bird. His hands moved with the careful clumsiness she had forgotten.

“Here you are, Magpie.”

“Why am I Magpie?”

“Because you collect shiny things.”

“I don’t.”

“You collected three buttons, a bottle cap, and Mrs. Fen’s silver earring.”

“I gave the earring back.”

“Eventually.”

He set the paper bird on her crown.

The child laughed.

The sound pierced Mara more deeply than the final telephone call.

Nothing important happened in those forty-seven minutes. No revelation, no farewell, no grand expression of love. A father and daughter waited for a train. They invented stories. They shared a currant bun.

Then sunlight folded inward, and the attic returned.

Mara sat very still.

“I want that hour,” she whispered.

“It is not an hour.”

“I want it anyway.”

“To keep?”

“Yes.”

“You cannot take the memory outside. Only what it teaches you.”

“What does it teach me?”

Orra smiled sadly. “That is not the curator’s decision.”

A bell rang somewhere below.

Mara stood.

“How much time has passed?”

“Enough.”

“My train—”

“Is still possible.”

They descended the iron stairs and returned through the galleries. As they walked, Mara noticed things she had missed before. Some bottles shone brightly. Others were almost dark. From behind the doors came fragments of ordinary life: dishes being washed, someone humming off-key, a child asking for one more story.

At the front desk, Orra placed a small brass token in Mara’s hand. A bird was stamped on one side and an hourglass on the other.

“What is this?”

“Admission.”

“For next time?”

“For whenever you notice the door again.”

Mara closed her fingers around it.

“Can you really give me five minutes?”

“Yes,” Orra said.

Mara looked up.

The curator opened a drawer beneath the desk and removed a tiny bottle filled with pale gold light.

“Five minutes spent watching dust turn in a sunbeam,” she said. “Lost by a poet in 1791. He would not resent your using them.”

“Why?”

“He believed time was meant to be wasted beautifully.”

Orra uncorked the bottle.

The gold light rose and settled over Mara’s shoulders like warm air.

“Go,” she said.

Mara ran.

Outside, the oranges were still rolling across the street.

The station clock showed five minutes before departure.

Mara raced through the crowd, down the platform, and onto the train just as the doors closed. She stood breathless in the aisle, one hand gripping a seat.

The train began to move.

Only then did she realize she had not thanked Orra.

Foxmere lay beneath steady rain when she arrived. The church bell was striking noon. Mara hurried uphill through streets she had known since childhood.

She reached the cemetery as the mourners gathered around the open grave.

Heads turned. Her cousin Elise stepped forward, but Mara shook her head and kept walking until she stood beside the coffin.

Rain darkened the polished wood.

The priest was speaking about eternity. Mara heard none of it.

She placed one hand on the coffin and felt the cold rain collect between her fingers.

“I’m sorry I’m late,” she whispered.

For a moment she was six years old, crowned in paper, waiting beside her father for a train that might never come.

Then she understood what the lost forty-seven minutes had taught her.

Her father’s life was not contained in their final call, nor was her love measured by the months she had stayed away. Regret was real, and it would remain real. But it was not the only truth.

There had also been currant buns.

Paper birds.

Snow on railway tracks.

A thousand ordinary hours, forgotten but not gone.

After the funeral, Mara went alone to her father’s house. She washed his blue cup and placed it on the shelf. She found his gray coat hanging by the door, one button loose. In the pocket was a silver bottle cap, polished smooth with age.

Mara laughed, though she was crying again.

That evening, she sat in his kitchen without turning on the lights. Rain tapped the window. The wall clock counted the seconds.

She did not hurry them.

Years later, when Mara walked down Bellweather Street, she sometimes saw the blue door and sometimes did not.

Whenever it appeared, she entered.

She never asked to borrow time again.

Instead, she brought Orra tea and listened to stories from the galleries. She learned that hours were rarely lost because they were empty. More often, they vanished because people had not understood their value while living them.

So Mara began to pay attention.

She watched water boil. She listened to unanswered telephones. She sat beside sleeping friends. When trains were delayed, she invented histories for strangers.

And on the mantel in her home, beneath a glass dome, she kept a paper bird.

It had cost her forty-seven forgotten minutes to find it.

It took the rest of her life to remember.
